chapter.title: The one equation

cards.body: A correctly drawn-up balance sheet always balances, and nobody had to get lucky to make that happen. Picture a house worth $300,000 with a $220,000 mortgage on it: **what you own minus what you owe is what's yours**, $80,000. A balance sheet is that same sum for a company, like a photo of its house taken on one day.
cards.simpler: A correctly made balance sheet always adds up exactly. That isn't luck. Think of a house worth $300,000 with a $220,000 loan on it. **What you own minus what you owe is what's yours**: $80,000. A balance sheet does the same sum for a company. It's like a photo of the company's house, taken on one day.

cards.prompt: Priya's flat is worth $250,000. She still owes the bank $180,000 on her mortgage. How much of the flat is really hers?

whyNot.a: That's what she owns, not what's hers: the bank's $180,000 is still inside that number.
whyNot.c: That adds the debt to the flat. Debt shrinks your share. It doesn't grow it.

cards.reteach: Think of the flat as a pie that Priya and the bank share. The bank's slice is the $180,000 she still owes. Her slice is whatever is left: $250,000 minus $180,000.

cards.title: Own, owe, yours
cards.body:
Accountants have a word for each part of the house. *Assets* are everything the company owns: cash in the bank, boxes in the warehouse, the delivery van parked out back. *Liabilities* are everything it owes: bank loans, the electricity bill it hasn't paid yet.

*Equity* is what's left for the owners once every debt is paid. It's the part of the house that belongs to you, not the bank.

Put them together and you get the one line every balance sheet follows: **assets = liabilities + equity**. Own equals owe plus yours. It's the same sum as the house, just moved around.
cards.simpler:
Accountants give each part of the house a name. *Assets* are everything the company owns, like cash in the bank, boxes in the storeroom and the delivery van. *Liabilities* are everything it owes, like a bank loan or an unpaid electricity bill.

*Equity* is what's left for the owners after every debt is paid. It's your share of the house, not the bank's. Together they make one rule: **assets = liabilities + equity**. Own equals owe plus yours.

cards.title: Rosa's Bakery, 31 December
cards.body: At closing time on 31 December, Rosa's Bakery owns $12,000 in the bank, $3,000 of flour, butter and unsold croissants, and an oven and van worth $45,000: **$60,000 of assets**. It owes $25,000 on a bank loan and $5,000 to the flour supplier: $30,000 of liabilities. That leaves $30,000 of equity, which is Rosa's share. Check: $30,000 owed plus $30,000 hers equals $60,000 owned, to the cent. *And yes, the croissants officially count as assets, at least until someone eats them.*
cards.simpler: At closing time on 31 December, Rosa's Bakery has $12,000 in the bank, $3,000 of flour, butter and unsold croissants, and an oven and van worth $45,000. That's **$60,000 of assets**. The bakery owes $25,000 on a bank loan and $5,000 to its flour supplier, so $30,000 of liabilities. The $30,000 left over is Rosa's share, her equity. Check: $30,000 owed plus $30,000 hers makes $60,000 owned. And yes, croissants count as assets until someone eats them.

cards.prompt: The Spoke & Chain bike shop's balance sheet shows total assets of $90,000 and total liabilities of $65,000. A coffee ring has smudged out the equity line. What did it say?

whyNot.a: That adds what it owes to what it owns. Equity is what's left after the debts, so you subtract.
whyNot.c: That's the assets total, not the owners' share: $65,000 of it belongs to the lenders.

cards.reteach: Equity is the leftover. Start with everything the shop owns, take away everything it owes, and whatever remains belongs to the owners: $90,000 minus $65,000.

cards.title: Why it can't be off by a cent
cards.body:
You'd think a sheet that always balances took careful work. It didn't. Equity is defined as the leftover, so it always fills the exact gap between what the company owns and what it owes.

Also, **every move touches two lines at once**. Borrow $10,000 and cash goes up $10,000 while the loan goes up $10,000. Spend that cash on a van and cash drops $10,000 while a $10,000 van appears. The totals don't change.

It's like swapping a $20 note for two $10s in your wallet. Different pieces. Same amount.
cards.simpler:
A sheet that always matches sounds like hard work. It isn't. Equity is the leftover, so it always fills the gap between what's owned and what's owed.

And **every move touches two lines at once**. Borrow $10,000 and cash goes up $10,000, but so does the loan. Spend it on a van and cash drops $10,000, but a $10,000 van appears. Totals stay put. It's like swapping a $20 note for two $10s. Same money.

cards.body: Sam opens a company's annual report, sees both sides of the balance sheet end at $4.2 million, and texts a friend: books look solid. But a company owing $4.1 million would balance just as neatly, with only $100,000 left for the owners. **Balancing proves the maths, not the health.** To spot this mistake, compare the size of equity with the size of the debts instead of checking whether the totals match.
cards.simpler: Sam opens a company's yearly report and sees both sides of the balance sheet end at $4.2 million. Sam texts a friend: the books look solid. But a company owing $4.1 million would match just as neatly, leaving only $100,000 for the owners. **Balancing proves the maths, not the health.** To avoid this mistake, compare how big equity is next to the debts, not whether the totals match.

cards.prompt: A café borrows $20,000 from the bank, and the money lands straight in its bank account. What happens to its balance sheet?

options.text: Assets go up $20,000 and liabilities go up $20,000, so it still balances.
Assets go up $20,000 and equity goes up $20,000, so the owners are richer.
It's out of balance until the loan is paid back.

whyNot.b: That mixes up owe with yours. Borrowed money belongs to the bank, so it sits in liabilities.
whyNot.c: That treats balancing as luck. Every move lands in two places at once, so the sheet never drifts.

cards.reteach: Every move lands in two places. Borrowed cash adds to what the café owns and adds the same amount to what it owes. Both sides grow by $20,000, so they still match.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Back at Rosa's Bakery on 31 December: **$60,000 of cash, oven, van and croissants = $30,000 owed + $30,000 hers.** That one line is the whole balance sheet: what she owns (assets) equals what she owes (liabilities) plus her share (equity). Her share is just the leftover, and every move touches two lines, so it always balances.
cards.simpler: Think back to Rosa's Bakery on 31 December: **$60,000 of cash, oven, van and croissants = $30,000 owed + $30,000 hers.** That one line is the whole balance sheet. What she owns (assets) equals what she owes (liabilities) plus her share (equity). Her share is the leftover, and every move changes two lines together, so it always matches.

cards.body:
Draw up your own tonight. Jot down roughly what you own (bank balance, car, laptop) and what you owe (card balance, loans). Subtract. That number is your equity, and you've just written your first balance sheet.

Tomorrow: why a balance sheet can't tell you what a company earned.
cards.simpler:
Try making your own tonight. Write down roughly what you own, like your bank balance, car and laptop. Then write what you owe, like a card balance or loans. Take the second number away from the first. **What's left is your equity**, and you've just made your first balance sheet.

Tomorrow: why a balance sheet can't tell you what a company earned.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now find the three totals on any balance sheet and show that what it owns equals what it owes plus the owners' share.

dubious_claims: 'Every balance sheet ever published balances to the cent': big companies usually publish figures rounded to thousands or millions, so 'to the cent' isn't literally true, and 'every one ever' is too sweeping, since some published balance sheets have contained errors.
repairedFrom.why: The 'In one breath' card only repeats the rule in abstract words, with no object, place or moment, and its strong 'Tomorrow' teaser is buried because the 'try' card comes after it.
repairedFrom.fix: Rebuild card 9 around Rosa's Bakery ('$60,000 of oven, van and croissants = $30,000 owed + $30,000 hers') and move 'Tomorrow: why a balance sheet can't tell you what a company earned' to be the last line of card 10.
